title: Building Blocks Overview
summary: A map of the standard toolkit — load balancer, cache, database, queue, CDN — and which problem each one solves, before going deep on any single piece.

slides.markdown:
Almost every system design answer reuses the same handful of parts: a **load balancer**, an **app tier**, a **cache**, a **database**, a **queue**, and a **CDN**. Knowing what each one solves — and when it's overkill — is the toolkit every other topic in this app goes deeper on.

Think of it like a kitchen's standard equipment: not every dish needs every appliance, but you should know what each one is for before deciding which ones this dish actually needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the standard building blocks, end to end
slides.markdown:
![The standard system design building blocks end to end](assets/building-blocks-overview.svg)

A request typically flows: client → **CDN** (for static assets) → **load balancer** → **app tier** → **cache** (checked before the database) → **database** — with a **queue** sitting off to the side for work that doesn't need to happen synchronously (sending an email, resizing an image).

This is the reference shape most designs are variations of — adding, removing, or scaling individual blocks based on the requirements.

assets.alt: The standard system design building blocks end to end

slides.sectionTitle: What each block solves: LB, app tier, cache, DB, queue, CDN
slides.markdown:
**Load balancer** — distributes incoming requests across multiple app servers so no single one is overwhelmed, and routes around unhealthy nodes. **App tier** — the stateless business-logic servers that actually process a request. **Cache** — an in-memory store (Redis, Memcached) that serves frequently-read data far faster than hitting the database each time. **Database** — durable storage of record; the source of truth. **Queue** — decouples producing work from processing it, so slow or bursty tasks don't block the request path. **CDN** — caches static content (images, JS, video) at edge locations near the user, cutting both latency and origin load.

Each block solves a distinct problem; reaching for one that doesn't match your actual bottleneck is wasted complexity.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: how a request actually flows through all of them
slides.markdown:
![A single request tracing through every building block](assets/request-flow.svg)

Trace one concrete request — a user viewing a product page: the CDN serves the page's images directly; the load balancer routes the HTML request to an available app server; the app server checks the cache for the product data first, and only queries the database on a cache miss; posting a review might additionally push a "send notification" job onto a queue instead of sending it inline.

Notice most of the path is optimizing for the common case (cache hit, static assets from CDN) while still having a correct, if slower, fallback.

assets.alt: A single request tracing through every building block

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: when you need each block vs when it's overkill for the scale
slides.markdown:
| Block | Add it when | Overkill when |
|---|---|---|
| Load balancer | More than one app server, or you need health-check failover | A single-instance MVP with negligible traffic |
| Cache | Read-heavy, with hot keys re-read far more than they change | Write-heavy data, or data too small to matter (a database index already handles it) |
| Queue | Work can happen asynchronously and bursts unpredictably | Every operation genuinely needs a synchronous result before responding |
| CDN | Meaningful static asset traffic, or a geographically spread user base | An internal tool with a handful of local users |

**How to decide:** add a block when a *specific, current* bottleneck justifies it — not because a "proper" system is assumed to have all of them.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading a system design diagram like an interviewer does
slides.markdown:
When you look at (or draw) a system design diagram, an interviewer is mentally checking each box against three questions: **What problem does this solve?** (If you can't answer, it's decoration.) **What happens if it fails?** (Is it a new single point of failure?) **Does its presence match the stated scale?** (A queue and three caching layers for 100 users a day is a red flag, not sophistication.)

Practicing this on other people's diagrams — including ones in this app — is one of the fastest ways to get better at building your own.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for every block regardless of the requirements
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A good system design answer uses a load balancer, cache, queue, and CDN — I should include all of them to look thorough."

**Why it's wrong:** every block you add is something you now have to justify, operate, and explain the failure modes of. An interviewer who asks "why is there a queue here?" and gets "...system designs usually have one" learns you added it as decoration, not as a decision — which is worse than a simpler diagram with clear reasoning behind every piece.

**Correct model:** each block should trace back to a specific requirement (see [Trade-Offs & Non-Functional Requirements](trade-offs-and-nfrs)). A design with three well-justified blocks beats one with six unjustified ones.

slides.sectionTitle: Where to go deep: pointers to the dedicated groups
slides.markdown:
This topic is the map, not the territory — each block gets its own dedicated deep dive elsewhere in this app: load balancing algorithms and layers, caching strategies and invalidation, database indexing and sharding, message queues and delivery guarantees, and CDN edge caching behavior.

Use this topic to know *which* deep dive is relevant to a given problem before you go there — recognizing "this is a caching problem" or "this is a load-balancing problem" is itself half the skill.
